teaser: Delacroix did not fight on the barricades. He painted this instead.
review_notes:
Delacroix's letter to his brother (October 1830): 'I have undertaken a modern subject, a barricade, and if I have not fought for my country, at least I will paint for her.' Given as a paraphrase in the lesson; check wording if it is ever shown as a direct quote.
State purchase in 1831 for 3,000 francs, then removed from view and returned to the artist's family; entered the Louvre in 1874.
Man in the top hat: long said to be a self-portrait, now generally rejected. Lesson says so.
Boy with pistols 'often said' to have inspired Gavroche in Hugo's Les Misérables (1862): a common claim, not proven.
Critics in 1831 finding Liberty dirty and vulgar (wording kept general, no quote).
Vandalism at Louvre-Lens in February 2013 (inscription in marker, removed the next day).
French 100-franc banknote with Delacroix and the painting, issued from 1978 into the 1990s.
Restoration completed in 2024 (our image is the post-restoration photograph).
Kneeling figure's clothes read as blue, white and red: the blue smock and red sash are clear in the image, the white is a small area of shirt.

lesson.text: Paris, July 27, 1830. King Charles X has just shut down the free press and dissolved the elected chamber. Printers walk out. By evening, stones are flying. July 28: streets are blocked with paving stones, carts and furniture, and the army fires. July 29: soldiers change sides, the palace falls. Three days. The king flees the country.

Eugène Delacroix, 32, already a famous painter, watched it happen and did not fight. That autumn he wrote to his brother that if he had not fought for his country, he would at least paint for her. He finished this huge canvas in about three months.

It measures 2.6 by 3.25 meters (roughly 8.5 by 10.5 feet), so the figures in front are life-size. A barricade is a wall thrown up across a street. Delacroix puts you at the foot of one, exactly where the crowd is about to land. They are coming over the top, toward you.
A riot is chaos. Yet this picture is easy to read in one second. Here is the hidden order.

lines.label: A pyramid
lines.text: The dead form the base, the fighters the sides, and the flag the tip. A triangle is the most stable shape there is. Delacroix uses it to hold a stampede together.

lines.label: The rising line
lines.text: From her bare foot on the rubble to her fist on the flagpole, one long upward push. Your eye climbs with it and ends on the colors.

lines.label: A look upward
lines.text: The wounded figure at her feet lifts their head toward her face. That gaze tells you where to look, and what she means to the people around her.

lesson.text: At the top of the pyramid stands someone who was not there in July. This woman is an allegory, an idea given a human body: Liberty herself. Her profile is straight out of an ancient Greek statue, and her red cap is the Phrygian cap, worn as a sign of freedom since the French Revolution of 1789.
Delacroix mixes two things painters had kept apart: a goddess-like symbol and real people in dirty street clothes, in the same smoke, on the same stones.

The blue, white and red flag had been banned in France for fifteen years. Under the returned kings, the official flag was plain white. Seeing the three colors fly again over Paris in July 1830 was a shock in itself, and Delacroix makes them the brightest patch of paint in the picture.
Around her, Delacroix chose his fighters with care. No two belong to the same world. He wanted the uprising to look like the work of a whole city, not of one class.

lesson.title: The people
lesson.text: Who follows Liberty? Meet four of them, from left to right.

spots.title: The worker
spots.text: Open shirt, apron strap across his chest, a saber in his fist. He is a factory hand or craftsman, the kind of man who built most of the barricades.

spots.title: The man in the top hat
spots.text: Jacket, tie and hat: city clothes, with a hunting gun. People long said this was Delacroix himself. Historians today doubt it.

spots.title: The kneeling figure
spots.text: Blue smock, red sash, a bit of white shirt: the flag again, worn on a body. The colors of the flag are scattered all over the canvas like an echo.

spots.title: The boy
spots.text: A street kid in a student's black cap, a pistol in each hand, mouth open in a shout. He is the only one running ahead of Liberty.

lesson.text: That boy had a long life ahead of him. More than thirty years later, Victor Hugo created Gavroche, the brave street child of his novel Les Misérables, and readers have linked the two ever since. As for the rest of the crowd, behind these four it dissolves into smoke, hats and bayonets: a few faces stand for thousands.

Where exactly are we? Delacroix invented this barricade, but he wanted no doubt about the city. He slipped a famous Paris landmark into the smoke, and on top of it, a tiny sign that the rebels are winning.
Somewhere in the haze stands the cathedral of Notre-Dame. Find its two towers.

spots.title: Notre-Dame
spots.text: The twin towers rise above the rooftops on the right. A tricolor flag, just a fleck of paint, flies from one of them: the cathedral has been taken.

lesson.text: The lower third is the hardest part to look at. A man stripped of his trousers on the left, two dead royal soldiers on the right. Delacroix gives the bodies of both sides the same weight. Liberty has to step over all of them. The picture cheers the revolution and counts its cost in the same breath.

The new government bought the painting in 1831 for 3,000 francs, then got nervous. A picture that makes revolt look glorious is awkward for whoever is in power. It was taken off view and spent years out of sight, part of that time back with Delacroix's family. It only entered the Louvre in 1874, after his death.

Many critics in 1831 were not kind. They found Liberty dirty and vulgar, more market woman than goddess. That was exactly the point. Delacroix belonged to Romanticism, a movement that preferred emotion, movement and color to calm, polished perfection. His brushwork stays loose, and the smoke is paint dragged quickly across the canvas.

For years, French people carried this painting in their wallets: it was printed on the 100-franc banknote, next to Delacroix's portrait. And in 2024 the real canvas came back from a long cleaning. Layers of yellowed varnish were removed, and the sky turned out to be far bluer than anyone alive had seen.

quiz.question: How long did the July 1830 uprising in Paris last?
quiz.explanation: The fighting ran from July 27 to July 29, after which the king fled.

quiz.question: What is an allegory?
options: An idea given a human body
A sketch made before a painting
quiz.explanation: The woman is not a real fighter: she is Liberty in human form.

quiz.question: Which building appears in the smoke on the right?
quiz.explanation: Its two towers show above the rooftops, with a tiny tricolor on top.

quiz.question: What did the government do after buying the painting in 1831?
options: Hung it in every town hall
Took it off view for years
quiz.explanation: An image that glorifies revolt made those in power uneasy, so it was hidden.

quiz.question: What shape organizes the composition?
options: A pyramid with the flag at the tip
A row of figures in a straight line
quiz.explanation: The dead form the base and the flag the top of a large triangle.

facts.text: Delacroix fought on the barricades before painting this picture.
facts.explanation: He watched the uprising without fighting, and said he would paint for his country instead.

facts.text: The red cap worn by Liberty is a symbol of freedom from the 1789 Revolution.
facts.explanation: It is the Phrygian cap, a revolutionary emblem.

facts.text: The painting has hung in the Louvre without interruption since 1831.
facts.explanation: It was hidden for years and only entered the Louvre in 1874.
